en: The Zen Oral Instructions of the Great Master Tiantai Zhiyi:

The Master said, "Regarding *ānāpāna-smṛti* (mindfulness of breathing), one should know that physical form and mind arise in mutual dependence through the breath. It is like fire depending on fuel for its smoke;
by observing whether the smoke is clear or turbid, one perceives the nature of the dryness or moisture [of the fuel]. By examining the breath, one discerns its softness..."
The coarse use of the mirror serves as a signpost for the true and the false.
Those who maintain it may, like those gazing at clouds to reach the shore or watching the bank to cross the river,
master the oar to recognize its mechanism and thus ensure the boat’s successful crossing.
The Master said: "When the body is at ease and the mind is upright, it is like oil being pure and a lamp being bright.
Therefore, if one wishes to guard the mind, one must first bring the body to rest.
As for bringing the body to rest:"
One should settle the bodily winds so that the functions of the winds do not become conflicted or disturbed.
What are the functions of the winds?

Within the body there are the circulating winds, the transverse-arising winds, the winds of the various joints, the winds of the hundred vessels, the winds of the sinews, the winds of strength, the winds between the bones, the winds of the waist, the winds of the spine, the upward-moving winds, and the downward-moving winds.
Thus, each stage of these winds has its own distinct portion and must not be confused;
if they are confused, they become thieves;
if they are excessive, they lead to madness, ruin, and cessation.
On a minor scale, the empty and the solid mutually oppress one another: the empty causes itching, while the solid causes pain.
When pain and itching afflict the body, what leisure is there to fix the mind on [the Dharma]?
As for those who are deranged and insane, they naturally have no words to speak.
In all matters of movement, stillness, and action,
one should first bring this thought to the fore before engaging in the task.
Otherwise, the coarse and the subtle will clash, and the new and the old will conflict.
If one attempts to prohibit misconduct through ritual alone, how can it be brought to an end?
Now, I shall briefly cite one instance as an example, for all others are of a similar nature.
Suppose, when about to take one's seat, one first forms this mental visualization:
"I shall sit there; from here, I shall go there.
As I take each step, I shall gradually extend my breath and slowly relax my body."
When the wind of stillness slightly arises, the wind of movement gradually departs;
it is the same for the other modes of deportment.
One who contemplates in this manner is said to have established the body.
The Master spoke in verse:
"Advancing and halting follow a sequence; The coarse and the subtle do not conflict.
Like a well-trained horse, It moves as if it were staying still."
One should always be able to exercise caution in this; as the Chan Master Anxinshenru said:
"Whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, one should always maintain mindfulness."
If one lies down too much, one becomes drowsy and dull;
if one stands too long, one becomes utterly exhausted;
if one walks too much, one becomes distracted and agitated, making it difficult to concentrate the mind on a single point.
Sitting has no such faults, which is why it is used so extensively.
The practitioner should dwell in a quiet and secluded place and sit in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*).
A woman should sit in the half-lotus posture with the body held upright and straight.
Relaxing the body and letting the four limbs be at ease,
one should arrange the skeletal structure so that the joints are properly aligned;
without leaning or bending, one should remove the robe and loosen the belt.
Whenever there is any unease or slight movement, one should immediately seize the essential point to bring it back to a state of equilibrium.
With composure, place the left hand upon the right hand,
ensuring that the tip of the little finger of the left hand rests against the base of the thumb of the right hand.
Lower the heads of the two thumbs of both hands;
as soon as they meet, release the jaw;
open the teeth slightly and raise the tongue subtly.
Exhale deeply four or five times.
Next, gaze steadily forward and slowly close the eyes gently,
ensuring that the eyelids are not pressed too tightly.
"Make sure that your eyes remain steady.
The Master spoke this verse to admonish him:
"In the three periods of entering, abiding, and exiting, It is like the kalpa of formation, abiding, and destruction."
"He who desires speed does not reach the goal; he who reaches the goal knows moderation. One should heed the words of the teacher.
There are four kinds of breaths which should be carefully distinguished.
First is wind, second is qi, third is panting, and fourth is breathing. That which has sound is called wind;
that which is congealed and obstructed is called qi;
that which enters and exits without being fully exhausted is called panting.
When there is no sound and no obstruction, and both inhalation and exhalation have reached their cessation, it is called "breath" (xi).
It is subtle and continuous, as if it were present;
yet to guard the labored breath is wearisome.
To guard the vital energy (prāṇa) leads to its coagulation;
to guard the wind (vāyu) leads to distraction;
to guard the breath (śvāsa) leads to concentration.
Master Wen’s family focused their mindfulness upon the center of their own navels, at the spot resembling a bean seed;
they removed their clothes and observed it intently to grasp its characteristics.
Thereafter, they closed their eyes, pressed their lips together, parted their teeth, and extended their tongues toward the palate.
He should cause the breath to be calm and even, and contemplate with single-minded concentration.
If external thoughts arise, he should collect them and bring them back.
If he does not see [the body] despite his mindfulness, he should again loosen his clothes and look at it.
Having thoroughly grasped its characteristics, he returns once more to the previous state.
Question: For what reason does he attend to the navel?
Answer: His breath exits from the navel, enters [the body], and is extinguished at the navel.
The navel is the point from which the breath emerges and ceases;
one contemplates the navel in order to understand impermanence.
Furthermore, the navel is the root source of the intestines and stomach.
By tracing back from the source along the path, one naturally perceives impurity.
Upon perceiving impurity, craving and desire cease.
In the context of the foundations of mindfulness, this constitutes the foundation of mindfulness of the body.
Within the six subtle gates, this serves as the locus for cessation.
Furthermore, at the very beginning of the consciousness-spirit’s entrustment to rebirth,
its root, which unites with the semen and blood, resides in the navel.
Therefore, when a person is born, they are held together only by the navel.
If a practitioner perceives the navel clearly, a natural sense of weary detachment (*nirveda*) arises, and they are liberated from bondage.
As the Sūtra says: "Wherever the mind goes, bind it there and observe with discernment."
This refers to the point where the roots of the inhalation and exhalation of the breath are at the navel.
Question: When fixing the mindfulness, there may be pain like the prick of a needle, or a sensation of tension like being pulled by a rope.
Sometimes there is an itch as if insects were gnawing;
sometimes it is cold as if being washed with water;
sometimes it is hot as if being scorched by fire.
When these various contacts or luminous deities have finally become utterly still, this is the "Lightning Flash" concentration (*vidyut-prabhā-samādhi*).
At that time, there are immeasurable similar phenomena;
the practitioner must not cling to any of them at all.
Simply by exerting effort with single-mindedness, one will naturally attain deliverance.
If one is not diligent, one will instead fall back into decline.
Question: Why is it that during the practice of counting the breaths, one suddenly forgets the count and knows only the breath?
Answer: Because the mind gradually becomes subtle, it ought to be focused on a single state of mind; for this reason, one loses count.
Previously, when the breath was one and the count was one, these two were simultaneous, and thus [the practice] was coarse.
Question: Why is it that one does not perceive the breath but perceives only the object?
Answer: Because the practitioner has already eliminated coarse observation, the breath gradually becomes subtle and thus is no longer seen. Some say:
Because [the breath] issues forth from all places where the pores are fully opened, there is no [specific] ear [for it].
The Master says that because the breath is subtle, it is not seen.
This statement regarding its dispersal through the pores—
Since it has already been granted that [the breath] exits, how could the nose-door alone not do so?
The statement that it is "subtle and unseen" refers to the state of focused mindfulness;
the statement that it "exits through the pores" refers to the state of unimpeded circulation.
Some say: when the breath is stilled and activity ceases, the mind-eye suddenly brightens for a moment like a flash of lightning;
one suspects this is the "lightning-flash samādhi."
The practitioner says:
"If one simply does not perceive the breath, it is because the breath is subtle;
that the eyes suddenly become clear is what people commonly call 'silent illumination' (mòrán)."
Prior to this stage, there are also minor bodily sensations that many people mistake for the joy and bliss of dhyāna.
The Master says: "These are minds associated with the ten wholesome actions; they do not belong to the higher realms."
"Passing through this section is entry into the realm of dhyāna;
only by treading on ice and facing a deep abyss can one cross over.
The Master said, "One who encounters it knows it for themselves; there is no need to speak of it."
The various masters all use this to test whether a person is sincere or insincere.
They say that those who claim to know [the breath] might, being of the class of deluded thoughts, instead become a source of harm.
The Master said: "If you suddenly see the breath return again,"
Counting from one as before, when one person must leave after sitting for a long time, the breath becomes manifest;
at that moment, one should follow it for about ten breaths.
Furthermore, after repeatedly passing about ten breaths, one may slightly move the hands and feet; next, move them according to the method of massage.
Then, open the eyes, proceeding from subtle to coarse, before finally rising.
During this time, by means of constant counting of the breaths, one merely has a vague awareness of them,
but no longer applies oneself with focused diligence.
When the teacher provides instruction, he constantly recites the verse concerning the sequential order of inhalation and exhalation.
When a practitioner of seated meditation asks about various illnesses, the Master instructs:
"Simply bind the mind to the object of focus and do not allow other conditions to arise; the illness will naturally subside.
For those who apply this method, even after three days, there are none who do not recover.
Question: When the mind is distracted and sees things erroneously, how can this be cured? Answer: It can be healed by concentrating the mindfulness.
Question: When the four great elements are in a state of increase or decrease, how can they be restored to equilibrium?
Answer: The movement and transformation of the mind arise from the presence of wind in a fan;
its coming to rest follows this same natural principle.
The Master’s constant instruction in his admonitions is that the true mind must be bound to the true object.
True reality arises in succession from true reality;
true reality flows into one another, naturally entering the principle of true reality.
Question: Once one has attained meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*), does one immediately enter the principle, or is there a sequence of stages (*bhūmi*)?
Answer: For those of sharp faculties, the mind becomes concentrated and they enter [the realization] immediately, yet there is no fixed stage.
For those of dull faculties, they must pass through all nine successive concentrations (*anupūrva-samāpatti*) until concentration is exhausted before they finally realize it.
Question: Why do non-Buddhists who cultivate meditative concentration up to the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*) not realize the principle?
Answer: The non-Buddhists who practice meditative concentration all remain stuck in the notion of a self.
Because the mind acts as an obstruction, they do not realize the principle.
Furthermore, that which is called "pain" arises from turbulent winds; it is caused by contending with external objects.
What is meant by "contending with the external"?
It refers to the mind departing while being pulled outward by manifest expressions.
It is like teaching a child to walk: one simply lets them go.
One must not pull or drag [the bowels].
Is it not to be carefully observed that those who desire rapid arrival [of the fetus] may fall into peril?
Urgency causes the "twisting wind" (jǎofēng) to arise.
This is due to the practitioner’s excessive application;
because the force of the wind has not been fully distributed,
whether one exceeds or falls short constitutes the first error.
As for "itching," it arises because when the breath is produced, the practitioner perceives it as ceasing;
and when the breath ceases, they perceive it as being produced.
This is because the mind is in opposition to the breath.
Therefore it is said that when one is neither discerning nor clear, "cold" arises from within due to the increase of the water element in the object of mindfulness regarding taste;
"heat" arises because the practitioner constantly harbors expectations, whereby the fire element increases.
The Master said: "Now, one who wishes to practice cultivation must necessarily possess the requisite capacity; one without such capacity cannot accomplish the task.
What is meant by 'capacity'?"
These are the so-called four minds:
first, firm faith, which means having deep faith in the teacher;
second, receiving and utilizing, which refers to the teacher’s Dharma.
Third, one should be diligent and constantly exert oneself.
Fourth, regarding skillful means, it refers to subtle transformation;
that is, the channels within the body are like the hundred rivers returning to the sea.
The heart is like a *kumuda* flower;
its four petals join together, each having ten *nāḍī* (veins),
which are intertwined and bound together, so that there are forty veins at the tip of the heart.
From its base, a single channel extends straight toward the navel;
it is called the udāna wind.
"Udāna" means "the middle."
Therefore, this channel is called the central channel (*avadhūti*).
At the beginning of sitting meditation, various external forms manifest:
they may take the shape of one's parents, teachers, monks, kings, beautiful women, lions, tigers, or wolves.
Such are the demons and spirits.
The practitioner should employ the visualization of the mind;
by brandishing the vajra-sword toward them, they will immediately depart.
Now, illnesses are of many kinds:
first, those caused by the body;
second, those caused by spirits.
Third, illness caused by the Māras;
fourth, illness resulting from improper regulation of the breath;
fifth, illness caused by karmic obstructions.
Now, one must recognize that the first cause of self-inflicted illness is sitting while leaning against a wall or a robe,
or lying down before the assembly has departed.
If this mind is indolent, Māra finds an opportunity;
it enters the body and becomes a disease, causing the person's back and spine to ache with pain.
This is called the "infectious disease" (*zhùbìng*), which is difficult to cure.
The practitioner should be cautious of this.
In the method of treatment, one uses the breath to cause the qi to flow from the head toward the spine,
passing along the sides of the bone joints and descending downward.
One must apply oneself with diligent mindfulness for the affliction to be dispelled.
As for the second ghost that causes illness:
when a person is sitting, their mind dwells upon various kinds of things.
Either hoping to gain some knowledge,
or desiring to know the fortune or misfortune of others,
the *duhila* spirit enters their body.
Through various manifestations, one may perceive auspicious or inauspicious events and know the states of others' bodies;
or one may know the auspiciousness, misfortune, goodness, and evil within a single family, a village, a settlement, a province, a district, or an entire kingdom.
Or it may appear as if it were a sage, yet it is not a sage;
these are all created by the aforementioned ghosts, so do not accept them.
If one does not exorcise them, they will eventually be able to kill a person.
Third, regarding Māra manifesting as illness:

when a person sits with thoughts of gain and profit in mind, Māra immediately manifests various garments, food, drink, the seven treasures, miscellaneous objects, and articles of offering for them; one should recognize this.
If one becomes aware [of this], it must be treated immediately;
if not treated, it enters the heart and becomes a disease that is difficult to cure.
As for the fourth disease: there are those who sit without understanding how to regulate their breath and thereby fall ill.
It causes the body to become parched, constricted, and emaciated.
Such a person is without fault and easy to treat.
The method of treatment employs the breath of universal cessation through correct mental application; this breath is called the "pervasive breath."
The method for its application is to cause the mind to abide in the breath.
One lets the breath flow from the head until it pervades the four limbs;
this is not understanding how to employ the breath.
It causes the sinews and vessels to wither and dry up so that the body lacks luster;
by causing these two breaths to flow downward from above and making the breath pervade the entire body,
it is called "pervasive breath" (vyāna) and "filling breath" (pūraka).
Because the breath has pervaded [the body] entirely, the body is restored to its natural state and can be used for cessation (*śamatha*).
What is meant by "cessation"?
To abide upright with a balanced mind, unmoving—this is called cessation.
Fifth, regarding those with illnesses caused by karmic obstructions:
their entire bodies are swollen and distended, and their complexions are unnaturally plump yet jaundiced.
Because the obstructions of such individuals are heavy and difficult to cure, they must perform repentance.
The method of treatment employs the "burning breath" (*jiao*) and the "extinguishing breath" (*xi*). What is meant by "burning"?
These two breaths do not involve taking external objects such as embers or other substances and placing them within the body.
Again, apply the mind to the visualization of the breath as burning embers.
Let the two breaths proceed from the head to the feet and through the four limbs,
circulating everywhere until the swelling is completely dissolved.
Return to using the mind to settle the breath and abide upright with a tranquil heart;
once the breath is restored to its natural state, one need only perform repentance.
Furthermore, there are four types of weakness where the limbs are limp and lack strength.
If both arms and both legs feel as though they are about to fall off,
or if one arm feels as though it is about to fall off,
the treatment is to use the "pervasive cessation of flowing qi" (piàn xī liú qì) to fill the four limbs; after a long while, the condition will naturally be cured.
If the left side of the mouth is depressed, direct the breath to the left;
if the right side is depressed, direct the breath to the right side.
If the left corner or right corner is depressed, follow the same method as above.
If there are chronic ailments such as carbuncles, cold-natured disorders, or heat-natured disorders,
one should employ the breath to cause it to flow downward so that the illness is extinguished.
All various minor ailments within the body are likewise treated by means of the breath.
If one has a cold disorder, one should employ hot breath to circulate it;
if one has a heat disorder, one should employ cold breath to circulate it.
For these remedial practices, each is treated by means of these two types of breath.
Furthermore, when walking, one must employ the breath.
If the feet feel light while the head feels heavy, this is the delusive thought of a haughty mind;
one should therefore still the mind of delusive thoughts.
One may still the haughty mind;
one may look downward with the mind.
If the feet are heavy and the head is light, it is the mind of one who feels compassion.
Furthermore, when practicing, one must apply the mind so that it is neither too high nor too low, causing the breath to become harmonious.
Using the breath, cause it to pervade both body and mind;

then, one enters the contemplation of universal clarity (*sāmānya-vidyā-vipaśyanā*), wherein one may contemplate the samādhi of the nature of the mind and the samādhi of the physical marks of the Buddha-body.
The characteristic of the mind is its fundamental basis.
As the Sūtra says: "When consciousness recognizes the mind and penetrates the source, there is no falsehood.
Regarding the method for treating dysentery: settle the mind below the navel.
If suffering from cold dysentery, practice warm breathing;
if suffering from heat, practice cool breathing, continuing until recovery.
As for the method of treating coughs, one should begin when a cough is about to arise.
After exhaling three times, settle the mind and perform internal contemplation.
When you feel like coughing, exhale the breath and let it out;
then, as before, settle the mind and correct yourself.
Regarding the method for treating swellings: cause the breath to cease and cut off its flow, gathering it so that it pervades the area.
While maintaining the mind in meditative concentration (*samādhi*) upon the swelling, pierce it to create a single opening.
By causing the breath to enter and exit through this opening, the ailment will be cured. This is the treatment for the ear.
Fill the vessel with water, place it outside the opening, and draw [the air] very slowly.
By pulling the breath out yourself, the ailment will naturally be cured in a short while.
When a person suddenly feels as though there is something inside the throat, about one or two inches long—
If the mind refuses to emerge, one must settle it upon the object so that the mind dwells in concentration.
Only then should one direct the mind in four directions and say within the mental ground:
"Both internal and external are empty; from where could illness arise?"
One must also understand emptiness (*śūnyatā*) so that [the affliction] is dispelled and departs of its own accord.
If one suddenly experiences shortness of breath while sitting in meditation, one should first exhale;
then, drawing the breath back in through the nose, let it fill the body before finally expelling it.
Thereafter, settle the mind within the center of the palm; before long, it will depart of its own accord.
This is the method for curing various ailments within the body with a single breath:
take the air through the nose and draw it back in until the breath fills the entire body.
Then, gently closing the mouth, follow the breath as it enters naturally and place this respiration there;
draw the mind straight down from within the bones to dwell outside the gate of impurity.
When sleeping, draw the breath inward to the soles of the feet.
Whether walking, standing, sitting, or reclining, one should constantly employ this mind.
Whenever there are various ailments in the four parts of the body, one must require this breath to circulate through them;
only then should one draw the vital energy (prāṇa) toward the specific location of the ailment.
If one enters and exits from the site of illness while remaining in emptiness without obstruction, one will immediately recover.
To treat cold illnesses, use warm breath;
to treat hot illnesses, use cool breath.
To treat diseases of the marrow, use the *dāo-xī* (knife-rest) method:
break the tips of the ten toes and also break the bones above the ankles so that they protrude; the patient will immediately recover.
To treat swellings on various parts of the human body, use the *dāo-xī* to break the joints between the ten toes, causing them to protrude through the openings.
The body is swollen and full; one breathes calmly from the soles of the feet upward.
When the body feels heavy, one breathes lightly; when the body feels light, one breathes heavily.
At the beginning of sitting, one counts the length and brevity of the breaths.
If external spirits enter through the nose, the heart rises straight up to the crown of the head and becomes steaming hot.
To expel them, one should close the mouth and contract the breath upward to the crown;
then, by drawing the breath back down, it ceases.
If it is not treated and both eyes become dark, what is this affliction?
If it is caused by a spirit,
the name of that spirit is Badhvida.
He stretched out his hand to cover the blind man's eyes and immediately recited the mantra:
*Puruṣapuṇḍarīka puṇḍarīka uṣapuṇḍarīka*. He recited it three times.
The eyes immediately open and become clear, returning to the state as when first seated.
If one attains the mind of subtle abiding (*sūkṣma-vihāra-citta*) but is touched by external factors such that the breath is blocked upward, the chest and abdomen swell, and one cannot sit in peace:
These are the six spirits within the body that have all rushed together to the chest.
This is the method for treating the ailment:
first, loosen the waistband, exhale long and inhale short for ten breaths.
Thereafter, recite the aforementioned mantra while focusing on the ānāpāna [breath] until the tenth [recitation], at which point recovery will be attained. If, during the initial sitting,
one attains the state of *sūkṣma-vihāra-citta* (subtle abiding mind) and is touched by others,
the vital energy may surge upward and strike the lungs, thereby causing illness.
Immediately, the lungs become distended for over a hundred days;
one then suffers from vomiting and is unable to consume food or drink.
This is caused by an external malevolent spirit entering the human body, known as the Bhūta spirit.
It is red in color, with six eyes and eight apertures, which may be large or small.
Furthermore, there are three minor deities named Hu-sou-xie,
who may transform their bodies into the form of infants.
Some take the form of a python,
their bodies being dark red or black;
these are the *Dhūlākṣa* spirits.
Its form may be large or small; recite this three times.
While sitting in meditation, one may experience pain in the body, joints, waist, or back, and feel as though one is being struck by a malignant spirit.
This is called "exorcising the affliction."
"What is this ailment?
This is called 'the six sense faculties playing throughout the entire body.
Before long, the ailment will be cured by straightening the head and torso, extending the body three times, and practicing the mindfulness of inhalation and exhalation (*ānāpānasmṛti*)."
At the beginning of his sitting, the six spirits were submerged in gloom.
Because an outsider came and disturbed them, the six spirits emerged from within his body.
Within each of his pores there was one spirit.
All [the spirits] come rushing in, causing a joyful agitation;
the body becomes bluish and swollen, making it impossible to sit.
The method for treatment is first to close the mouth and contract the breath upward.
Second, draw the breath back through the entire body downward. Then,
recite the aforementioned mantra to command the *ānāpāna* (inhalation and exhalation),
and further list the names of the malevolent spirits and ghosts.
Ānāpāna-vyūha is immediately resolved.
Furthermore, it is said that exhalation is called "peace" (āna).
One who practices ānāpāna counts only the exhalations.
If, during the initial sitting, there are those who experience agitation or restlessness, it will not persist for long.
As for the method of treatment, first instruct them in *ānāpāna* (mindfulness of breathing).
As for confused speech, one should simply cease it as soon as it occurs.
At the beginning of sitting meditation, if fire should arise within the body, it is not a cause for concern.
As for the method of treatment: from outside in the darkness, bring fire inside without letting him know or hear it.
Place a basin over his head and have those sitting nearby chant:
This is the "Great Fire Arising" [practice]: open your eyes and do not look for three full rounds, then stop.
During the initial sitting, if water should emerge from within the body, it is not a cause for concern.
As for the method of treatment: fill a basin with water, ensuring that no one hears or knows of it.
Hold water in the mouth and sprinkle it on the face while opening the eyes; do this three times and then stop.
During the initial sitting, if one repeatedly experiences physical contact, the mind may become agitated by the arrival of others, causing a sense of constriction within the heart.
Immediately upon feeling [the abdomen],
one finds that the lower functions of defecation and urination are obstructed;
this is because the six deities within the body have all descended and emerged, thereby giving rise to the ailment.
The method of treatment is to contract the breath and direct it downward, then draw it back upward.
Recite the mantra while practicing *ānāpāna* (mindfulness of breathing) until the ailment is cured. This is the method for applying the mind when about to go to the toilet;
when excreting either feces or urine, one may imagine that all illnesses are being expelled.
Furthermore, when the practitioner’s mind attains a slight awakening to its profound meaning,
they gradually understand it and their heart rejoices; yet,
by over-exerting their deliberation, they again encounter the affliction of weariness.
The practitioner should employ wisdom to deliberate:
when it is not appropriate to rest, one should rest; when it is appropriate to observe, one should observe.
When resting and observing accord with what is suitable, one will be able to remain for a long time.
The manifestations of fatigue are numerous;
even when one suffers from headaches or a feeling of fullness in the chest, all such conditions are treated with *ānāpāna* (mindfulness of breathing).
The method for treating headaches is as follows: inhale through the nose and exhale the breath gently through the mouth.
If one perceives a sensation of pain in the head and the breath is faintly exiting through the mouth,
and when the mind is subtle, refined, relaxed, and harmonious,
one should exhale the breath three times; at that point, one will naturally yawn.
In this manner, draw in the breath; if a yawn does not occur after ten [breaths], headache will be cured.
This is the method for treating the condition of fullness of qi within the abdomen:
inhale through the nose and exhale by drawing the breath out slightly through the mouth.
Focus the mind on the stifled qi within the abdomen and cause it to exit through the mouth; when afflicted by illness, one should practice *aiqi* (forced exhalation).
If the affliction arises when the abdomen is extremely full and congested, [one should likewise apply this method].
One should lie on one's back with the limbs extended and, using the hands, lightly stroke over the skin of the abdomen;
this must be massaged ten or five times. There will then be a sensation of gas escaping from the throat.
Return once more to sitting upright and draw the breath as in the previous method of treatment.
If the mind becomes compliant and subtle— even after ten or twenty years of affliction from accumulated vital energy (prāṇa)—
then in a single day and night, the mind and breath will become compliant and the vital energy will become harmonized.
Neither lax nor hurried, neither coarse nor subtle;
when balanced and properly regulated, all ailments will be cured.
If one [observes] whether the breath is coarse or subtle, slow or rapid—
If the regulation is not properly achieved, the condition will ultimately fail to be cured.
If the exhalation has sound, it is called coarse and rapid;
if the exhalation is as if about to cease without continuing, it is called subtle and slow.
It is better if it is fine and slow.
Furthermore, when the abdomen is full and one feels oppressed by gas,
drawing the breath out long will only increase the affliction.
Exhale so that it is neither too long nor too short, making it balanced, harmonious, and appropriate.
When this is achieved, the ailment will surely be cured.
This is the method for treating ailments by regulating the breath.
It treats all ailments of the intestinal wind.
Furthermore, those who practice seated meditation and attain a state of harmony and well-being will find all their illnesses cured.
Moreover, when entering seated meditation, one should not harbor sorrow, anger, or affliction, but should instead attain a refined and subtle concentration of mind.
One will inevitably suffer from respiratory ailments;
when counting inhalations, even that counting becomes a condition for respiratory illness.
Furthermore, practicing concentration by taking the five viscera as one's object also results in illness.
Even when reciting sutras, if one joins phrases together without regard for the natural flow of the text, or if inhalation and exhalation are irregular—
such as exhaling at improper times or inhaling at improper times— it will result in illness;
all such cases should be treated according to the methods previously explained.
Furthermore, when treating a headache, one must not treat abdominal distension;
when treating abdominal distension, one must not treat a headache.
To treat both ailments simultaneously will only further increase the affliction.
If the qi within the head is extreme when treating that affliction,
one should inhale through the nose while opening the mouth wide and gently draw the qi out.
Furthermore, those who practice diligent seated meditation often experience an abundance of qi.
If one suffers from ailments of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), one should habitually treat them by exhaling through the mouth; after practicing this for a long time,
when the teeth become cold and the mind attains a state of refinement and subtlety,
one should inhale through the nose and then likewise gently draw the breath out through the nose to treat it.
If the mind has become pliant and subtle, one should treat all ailments of the vital energies (*prāṇa*) entirely by means of inhalation and exhalation through the nose.
Furthermore, one may employ the method of counting the breaths, taking the afflicted area as the object of focus in accordance with the breath.
Furthermore, when entering [the state of concentration], one does not take the inhalation as an object, but takes only the exhalation as an object.
If one cultivates insight (vipaśyanā) to an excessive degree, the mind becomes agitated;
if one delights in emptiness (śūnyatā) to an excessive degree, the mind becomes sunken.
A practitioner of dull faculties should constantly and skillfully observe and contemplate in order to remedy this affliction.

Furthermore, if a practitioner of seated meditation, while the mind is being regulated within the body or among the five viscera, allows the mind to come and engage with external objects, or if they claim that the concentrated mind within the five viscera comes to engage with objects, such a person who exerts themselves in sitting practice will soon fall ill.
It can cause the vital energies (*prāṇa*) within the five internal organs (*pañca-dhātu*) of the practitioner to arise and become connected with external objects,
causing the person to contract a sudden cramping illness.
The method for treatment is to visualize the upper and lower parts of the body as empty.
One should form the mental image that everything from the wooden tube-like appearance up to the seat,
as well as the ground itself, is entirely empty;
all the breath within the body is made to descend, enter the earth, and depart.
If the mind is compliant and well-adjusted, the illness will be cured before long.
Once the patient has recovered from the ailment, one should instruct them to observe the object at the ankle joint.
Furthermore, the patient must be taught: "You contracted this illness because of mental error."
It is said that [the mind] resides within the body;
yet mental factors do not exist outside the body nor inside the body.
You should understand that they arise in accordance with their respective objects of perception.
Furthermore, when a person sitting in meditation contemplates an object,
the mind perceives it as a visual form.
Moreover, when that person abides in meditative equipoise, [the same occurs].
There is a radiance that illuminates the objective field;
one does not know that this is the radiance of the mind or the radiance of the intention,
which emerges from within the clarity and abides upon the objective field.
Such a person will before long suffer from eye pain,
causing the eyes to become dim and aching.
The method for treatment is to take the mind and focus it upon the eyes.
The mind observes that while the eyes are closed, such a thought arises;
since the method of seeing requires the eyes to be open and looking,
one now knows that when the eyes are closed, it is not the eyes that see.
Furthermore, when one contemplates the eye, one perceives the luminosity within the objective field.
When turning the contemplation upward toward the eye, this mind and its mental factors emerge from that luminosity;
yet these mental phenomena do not abide internally, nor do they abide externally, nor do they abide in between.
Since the eye is a mental phenomenon, it arises according to the object perceived by the mind;
furthermore, it does not exist within, without, or in between the two.
When one contemplates in this way, the deluded, provisional mind [is seen through].
All ailments shall be eliminated; the ailment of the eyes shall likewise be eliminated.
Furthermore, when sitting, one must not allow the waistband of the robe to be too tight, lest it cause the person to suffer from the obstruction of the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
Furthermore, if those seated attain meditative concentration of a higher stage,
they must not allow thoughts of good or evil to arise within that state;
this causes headaches and afflictions, so one must be careful to avoid it.
These various afflictions are to be treated according to the methods described above.
Furthermore, while seated, the person may see dust arising upon the objective field,
appearing as dense as if a spinning wheel were turning.
This person, afflicted by a wind disorder, is unable to cultivate the meditative concentrations of the higher stages,
which may cause them to go mad;
they can only practice the mindfulness of the body.
One should employ the skillful means of contemplative practice to treat the ailment of wind;
only after it has been cured can one learn the concentrations of the higher stages.
If one enters a shallow concentration and is disturbed by external sounds or tactile sensations, [the concentration will be lost].
If there is some physical contact with the body,
one immediately perceives it upon emerging from meditative absorption, and it does not become a source of affliction;
however, if the mind harbors resentment, malice, or vexation, then it becomes an affliction characterized by the swelling of the vital breath (*vāyu*).
If one enters a profound meditative absorption and there is a contact with a loud sound,
although the sound is external, it occurs within the body;
or the sound may be upon the objective sphere.
When such a person wishes to emerge from meditative absorption, they are unable to do so;
their mind remains within the body, and being terrified, their spirit becomes disoriented and confused before they can finally emerge.
Consequently, this causes the person to suffer from abdominal distension.
Or, if one suffers from sudden diarrhea or falls ill due to physical contact with something harmful,
it is also like this;
the method of treatment is likewise to practice breath regulation according to the previous method.
If anger or resentment arises, it cannot be cured. Sometimes,
while sitting down for the first time after killing someone,
if one suffers from the obstruction of feces and urine or upward-moving gas that is pulled back downward, [the following should be done].
Upon reciting the mantra of *ānāpāna*, he was immediately cured.
At the beginning of his seated meditation, various kinds of phenomena arose, and people came to disturb him.
Some slandered the Buddha-dharma using foreign and Chinese dialects that others could not understand.
This is the evil spirit named Dohilā who has entered the body;
by reciting the aforementioned mantra, one will immediately recover.
The body of the spirit Dohilā is yellow.
The breath is sometimes large and sometimes small.
The method for curing sudden pain in the body by practicing *ānāpāna*—inhaling (*āna*) and exhaling (*apāna*)—is as follows.
Question: Why does a person practicing *ānāpāna* experience sudden pain throughout the entire body?
One teacher said:
"It is because one has eaten too much and the food has not yet been digested, yet one restrains the mind; because the breath is coarse while the thoughts are subtle, it results in this state.
The method for treatment is to reduce one's food for two or three days."
Regulate the breath to make it long and attentively take the out-breath as the object.
After sitting for two or three days, one will recover.
A certain master said:
If mindfulness is held too tightly, the breath becomes constricted and illness arises.
The method for treatment is to visualize the body as being like the steam rising from rice cooking over a steamer;
then, visualize a wind arising from within the navel and exiting through the mouth.
The "gate of the face" refers to the mouth.
By repeatedly blowing forcefully with the breath from the body until it is dispersed,
the bodily pain will immediately heal once it has been dispersed.
For several days, one must consume rich and fatty foods and strictly avoid exposure to wind.
Furthermore, regarding the method of treatment:
before eating, one must remain in a private room and strictly avoid hearing any sounds.
Relax the four limbs and harmonize the breath at the mouth of the nose;
after sitting for two or three days, the ailment will be cured.
It is further said that this is because the *vāyu* (winds) were still vigorous when one first began to sit.
If one does not employ skillful means, the body will immediately seize up as if in a state of stagnant wind (*sthita-vāyu*).
This occurs because the stationary wind contends with the moving wind (*gati-vāyu*) for power.
To treat this, one must move the body, starting slowly and gradually increasing the pace until it reaches a distance of about five *li*.
Returning again from urgency to relaxation,
he sat down and sighed deeply four or five times.
He loosened his four limbs and released his mind, remaining thus for the duration of a meal.
Furthermore, draw the breath in two or three times without allowing the ears to hear the sound.
Then, relax the mind as before for the duration of one meal.
After that, collect the mindfulness until the end of the sitting session, and the affliction will be cured.
The Oral Instructions on Meditation by the Great Master Zhizhe of Tiantai
